t.caves of maresha and bet guvrin in the j:
Beneath the low hills of the Judean lowlands, the Shephelah, lies a city of caves. Maresha was an important town of the Iron Age and the Hellenistic period, and its inhabitants carved thousands of chambers into the soft chalk beneath their houses: cisterns, olive presses, stables, quarries, burial caves and columbaria, rooms with hundreds of niches, probably used for raising pigeons. Nearby Bet Guvrin, known to the Romans as Eleutheropolis, became a major city in later centuries. The national park and its caves were listed by UNESCO in 2014 as a microcosm of the land of the caves.

The highlights include the bell caves, huge bell-shaped chambers created by quarrying chalk from the early Islamic period, with walls rising to over twenty metres and light streaming through small openings at the top, an eerie and beautiful space. The Sidonian burial caves have colourful wall paintings of animals and hunting scenes from the Hellenistic period. There is also a Roman amphitheatre, and in some caves visitors can take part in archaeological digs.

The area lies within Israel, in the rolling hills between Kiryat Gat and the Hebron hills, with farmland, vineyards, forests and kibbutzim. The roads are generally good, with light traffic outside towns. Summer is hot and dry, winter mild with some rain, and spring brings wildflowers to the hills. The nearby kibbutz of Beit Guvrin and the town of Kiryat Gat have services, including fuel and food. Before travelling, check the current security situation and travel advice, as conditions in the region can change quickly, and the area is close to the line separating Israel from the West Bank.

The caves are cool inside, a welcome relief on a hot day, but the paths can be uneven, and some caves require going down steep stairs. Bring water and sturdy shoes. The park has a visitor centre with information and toilets. If you have time, the nearby Tel Lachish, another important biblical site, and the vineyards of the Judean hills are worth a visit. Combine the visit with Jerusalem, about an hour away, for a day of history spanning thousands of years.
t.tel beer sheba@31.2,34.8:
Tel Beer Sheba is a mound on the edge of the modern city of Beersheba, in the northern Negev desert of southern Israel, and it holds the remains of an Iron Age town that has been excavated and partially reconstructed. With Megiddo and Hazor, it forms the UNESCO site of the Biblical Tels, recognized for their importance in understanding the cities of the biblical era. The name Beersheba appears many times in the Bible, associated with Abraham and the wells he dug in the desert.

The site is fascinating for its planning. The town was laid out with a ring road and streets radiating from the gate, houses built against the walls, and storehouses near the entrance. Its water system, a deep shaft and cisterns cut into the rock, shows how the inhabitants survived in a dry land. A large horned altar, found dismantled and reused in the walls, has been reconstructed, and a copy stands on the site. From the top, there is a view over the desert and the modern city, and an observation tower gives a wider panorama.

The Negev is a land of open spaces and long roads. Beersheba is the gateway to the desert, and from here roads run south to Mitzpe Ramon and the Ramon crater, east towards the Dead Sea and Masada, and west towards the coast. The desert roads are generally well surfaced and straight, with long views, but heat is serious from May to October, often above thirty-five degrees, so start early and carry plenty of water. Sandstorms can reduce visibility, and wind can be strong. Before travelling, check current security advice for the region, which can change quickly.

Beersheba, five kilometres away, is a large city with fuel and all services, and its old Ottoman quarter has some interesting buildings. The Bedouin market, traditionally held on Thursdays, was once a famous sight, though it has changed over the years. The area around the tel includes a Bedouin town, Tel Sheva. In the evening, the desert light turns gold and the heat begins to ease, and the stones of the ancient town glow in the setting sun.
t.haluza@31.1,34.7:
Halutza is a ghost of a city in the sand. Founded by the Nabataeans as a waystation on the incense route from Arabia to the Mediterranean, it grew in the Roman and Byzantine periods into the most important city of the Negev, known in Greek as Elusa, with a theatre, churches and a famous school of rhetoric. Then it faded, the sand moved in, and today only fragments of walls, a small theatre and the remains of churches poke out of the dunes south-west of Beersheba. It is part of the UNESCO-listed Incense Route and desert cities of the Negev, along with Avdat, Mamshit and Shivta.

The Nabataeans were masters of desert survival, collecting every drop of rain in cisterns and channels, and their trading network carried frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia to the ports of Gaza and beyond, making them rich. At Halutza, the remains are less spectacular than at Avdat or Shivta, but the setting, among the shifting sand dunes of the western Negev, is evocative and lonely.

The riding in the Negev is about light, space and heat. Roads are long and straight across the desert, with wide views and few curves, and the surface is generally good on main roads. Off-road tracks lead to the archaeological sites, but they can be sandy and soft, so check conditions before venturing off the tarmac. Wind can be strong, and dust storms are possible, especially in spring. Summer temperatures are high, so ride early or late in the day and carry plenty of water.

Beersheba, about twenty-two kilometres away, is the main city of the Negev, with fuel, food, lodging and every service you might need. Ofakim and Yeruham are smaller towns nearby. Beersheba has its own ancient site, Tel Be'er Sheva, also listed by UNESCO, and a lively Bedouin market tradition.

The desert here has a stark beauty, with dunes, low hills and the occasional acacia tree, and in winter, after rain, it can turn surprisingly green, with wild flowers carpeting the ground. The light at dawn and dusk is extraordinary, turning the sand gold and pink. Security conditions in the region can change, so check current advice before travelling, and stay on marked routes. Halutza will not overwhelm you the way Avdat does, but out here among the dunes, with the wind moving sand over Byzantine stones, it has a lonely dignity of its own.
t.shivta@30.9,34.6:
There is no water at Shivta, and yet a town of some size thrived here, in the middle of the Negev desert, for several centuries. Its people collected every drop of rain that fell on the surrounding hills and channelled it into cisterns, and they grew grapes, wheat and olives in the dry valleys around. Shivta began as a Nabataean settlement on the trade routes between Arabia and the Mediterranean, and it reached its peak in the Byzantine period, when it had three churches, houses, wine presses and streets of stone. It is part of the Incense Route listed by UNESCO, with the desert cities of Avdat, Haluza and Mamshit.

The ruins are remarkably complete. Walls stand to a good height, the churches still have their apses, some with traces of painted decoration, and you can walk through streets and courtyards as if the inhabitants had only just left. The site is isolated, in a military area near the Egyptian border, and visitors are few. The desert around is a wide expanse of brown hills, dry riverbeds and scattered acacia trees, with an extraordinary silence and a sky full of stars at night.

The riding to Shivta is an adventure. The access road leaves the main road from Beersheba to Nitzana and runs through the desert, with long straights and gentle bends. Surfaces are mostly sound, but there is sand on the road in places, and some routes cross military zones where you must not stop. Summer heat is extreme, so ride early in the morning or in the evening, and carry plenty of water. Winter is milder but can bring sudden rainstorms that flood the dry riverbeds.

The nearest services are limited. Midreshet Ben-Gurion, about fifteen kilometres away, is a small community with a field school and a few shops, near the grave of David Ben-Gurion, overlooking the Zin valley. For reliable fuel, Yeroham or the larger towns are safer. Israeli food in the desert means hummus, falafel, salads and strong coffee. Before travelling, read up on local safety and road access. When you arrive, take time to climb onto a wall or a rooftop, look across the ruins to the desert, and imagine the patience it took to make a life here.
t.choirokoitia@34.8,33.3:
Long before the Greeks, the Phoenicians or the Romans arrived in Cyprus, people lived on a hillside above the Maroni river in the southern part of the island, in round stone houses with flat roofs, packed close together inside a defensive wall. Choirokoitia is a Neolithic settlement dating back to around the seventh millennium BC, one of the most important prehistoric sites in the eastern Mediterranean. The inhabitants farmed, herded animals and buried their dead under the floors of their houses. Several of the round houses have been reconstructed near the entrance, giving a vivid sense of how they lived. The site received UNESCO recognition in 1998.

The village of Choirokoitia, below the site, has its own history, including a battle in 1426 when the Mamluks defeated the army of the Lusignan king of Cyprus, Janus, who was captured and taken to Cairo. The surrounding landscape is dry and rugged, with terraced hillsides, carob and olive trees, and views down toward the sea. Not far away, the village of Lefkara, famous for its lace and silverwork, sits in the hills on the road toward the Troodos mountains.

The site is conveniently close to the main A1 motorway between Limassol and Larnaca and Nicosia, which makes it easy to reach but not particularly interesting to ride to. The fun begins when you head inland. The roads toward Lefkara and up into the Troodos foothills twist and climb through villages, vineyards and pine forest, with plenty of curves and good views. The Troodos roads, higher up, are some of the best riding in Cyprus, though narrow and sometimes busy with tour buses. Summer heat is intense, so ride early, and remember that Cyprus drives on the left.

Choirokoitia village and nearby Kofinou have small shops and cafés, and fuel stations are found along the motorway and in larger villages. The site itself is exposed, with little shade, so bring water and a hat. The path climbs fairly steeply up the hill, so wear comfortable shoes if you can. Look at the reconstructed houses first, then walk up through the excavated area to the top, from where you can see the whole valley. Afterwards, ride up to Lefkara for a coffee and a slice of something sweet in the square.
t.painted churches in the troodos region@3:
From the outside they look like barns: low stone buildings with steep pitched roofs of flat tiles, sometimes covered by a second wooden roof to keep off the snow. Inside, every surface glows with Byzantine and post-Byzantine frescoes. The painted churches of the Troodos mountains in Cyprus, nine of them inscribed in 1985 and a tenth added in 2001, form one of the richest collections of Byzantine painting anywhere.

The church of Panagia tou Araka at Lagoudera has frescoes from the late twelfth century, of extraordinary quality, while the church of the Holy Cross at Pelendri has fourteenth-century paintings. Each church has its own character, and visiting several gives a sense of how painting evolved over centuries. Many are kept locked, with a key holder in the village, so be patient and ask around.

The Troodos mountains rise to nearly 2,000 metres at Mount Olympus, and the landscape is a mix of pine forests, terraced vineyards, orchards and villages perched on steep slopes. In summer the mountains are cooler than the coast, and in winter they can be snowy. The villages produce wine, including the sweet Commandaria, zivania, a strong spirit, and smoked meats like lountza.

Riding in the Troodos is a joy. The roads are winding and steep, with endless curves through forests and villages, and views over the island to the sea. Traffic is light, except at weekends when locals head to the mountains. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel, fallen rocks and slow vehicles. Remember that Cyprus drives on the left, and that mountain roads can be narrow and blind.

Fuel is available in the larger mountain villages, but stations are spread out, so fill up when you can. Limassol, twenty-seven kilometres away as the crow flies but much further by road, has all services. Food in the mountain tavernas is excellent: meze, halloumi, grilled meats and local wine.
t.saint hilarion monastery tell umm amer@3:
Saint Hilarion was born around 291 in a village near Gaza and grew up to be the founder of monasticism in Palestine. He studied in Alexandria, was inspired by the desert hermit Anthony, and returned home to live a life of such strict simplicity that disciples followed him and settled around him. The monastery that grew up here, at the site known today as Tell Umm Amer, became one of the largest in the Middle East, with churches, a bathhouse, hostels and workshops, and it functioned for several centuries until the seventh century. Hilarion himself eventually left, wandered through Egypt, Sicily and Dalmatia and died in Cyprus around 371, but the monastery kept his name.

The site lies in the central Gaza Strip, near Nuseirat, and the mosaics and ruins of the monastery were included in UNESCO's World Heritage list in 2024, at once also placed on the list of sites in danger. Check official travel advice, local news and the situation on the ground before planning anything, and do not travel here on the strength of a map pin.

For a rider interested in the story, there are other places that carry it. Hilarion is remembered in Cyprus, where a castle on the Kyrenia range bears his name, and the Negev ride the route list pairs with this one, to the Nabataean desert city of Mamshit, shows a landscape of the same world, in the same period, with the same sense of long caravans and thin water.

When the situation allows, the site is meant to be experienced slowly, on foot, with someone who can read the mosaics and the history of a landscape where people have lived and prayed for thousands of years. Until then, it stays on the map as a place to know about, and to hope for.
t.church of timios stavros@34.9,33.0:
The painted churches of the Troodos mountains look plain from outside. Squat stone boxes with steep timber roofs, built that way to shed the snow, they hide inside some of the finest Byzantine frescoes in the Mediterranean, and nine of them were listed by UNESCO in 1985, with a tenth added later. The Church of Timios Stavros, the Holy Cross, at Pelendri, is one of the group, with frescoes from the fourteenth century that show scenes of the life of Christ, in the dark blues and ochres of the period, and an interior lit by only a little daylight so that the figures seem to glow.

The villagers were not wealthy, but they were devout, and in the long centuries of Frankish and Venetian rule, when Cyprus was a Latin kingdom with a Greek Orthodox population, the churches were a way of keeping their faith and art alive. Local donors appear in some of the paintings, kneeling at the feet of saints, a touch that makes the past feel intimate. The churches are usually kept locked, and a caretaker or a neighbour will fetch the key if you ask, and a small donation is welcome.

Pelendri is a hill village at about a thousand metres, on the south side of the range, with stone houses, a café and a beautiful old square, and Kyperounta is a larger village nearby, set among vineyards. This is the Commandaria country, where a sweet dessert wine has been made since the Middle Ages, said to be the oldest named wine still in production. Fuel is easier in Limassol on the coast, but mountain villages often have a pump, and Platres, a few kilometres off, has services.

The riding is a pleasure. The roads climb from the coast through pine, cedar and golden oak, with hairpins, smooth asphalt and sudden views over the island, and traffic is light, apart from weekend visitors. Fog and cold are possible at height, and snow falls in winter, so spring and autumn are best. In April the scent of herbs fills the air, and in October the grape harvest is under way. Ask for a coffee under the plane tree in the square and listen to the village.
t.church of ayia sotira@34.9,33.1:
This point lies in the northern foothills of the Troodos range, in a landscape of dry stone terraces, carob and olive trees, and villages that tilt down towards the Nicosia plain. What I can say is that the villages around it, Peléndri and Kyperoúnta among them, belong to one of the richest church regions in the eastern Mediterranean. The Troodos painted churches, ten of them on the UNESCO list, are small, steep-roofed stone buildings that hide Byzantine frescoes inside, and one of them, the Timios Stavros, stands at Peléndri.

For a rider, the pleasure is the slope. Roads here climb in long, tidy bends from the plain, with the temperature falling as you go, and the smell changes from dust and thistle to pine and warm resin. The surface is generally decent but sun-bleached, and gravel gathers on the inside of tight turns, particularly after the winter rains. Ride on the left, which catches continental riders out for the first ten minutes, and watch the goat and sheep droppings on the tarmac. Spring is the best season, when the hills are green and the wildflowers are out; summer is hot enough that you will want to ride early, and the heights stay cooler than Nicosia by many degrees.

The mountains behind are geologically unusual. Troodos is an ophiolite, a piece of ancient ocean floor pushed up onto land, and that is why the island had copper in the first place, and where the name of Cyprus and its metal come from in the ancient world. Highest point is Olympus at about 1,950 metres. Further up the villages make wine, and the Commandaria dessert wine, a sweet one with a thousand years of history, comes from slopes around Kyperounta and Peléndri among others.

Do not expect pumps in the smallest hamlets. The nearest larger town in the data is Tséri, on the plain, and Nicosia itself is not far; fill the tank before heading into the hills. Coffee in a village kafeneio, strong and sweet, costs very little and comes with a view of the mountain and an old man with an opinion about it. Leave time in the afternoon, because the light on the stone is at its best then.
t.paphos@34.8,32.4:
The ride that brings you here starts in Paphos but belongs, for a while, to Aphrodite. Kouklia, a village on the southwest coast of Cyprus, sits on the site of Palaepaphos, the old Paphos, where the goddess of love was worshipped for well over a thousand years before the Romans arrived. Ancient writers placed her birth in the sea off this coast, and a rock offshore near here is still called Aphrodite's Rock. The sanctuary was a pilgrimage centre across the Mediterranean, and pilgrims travelled from Greece, Egypt and Phoenicia to reach it.

The modern Paphos is a different animal, a lively harbour town with the Roman mosaics of the Kato Paphos archaeological park, tourist bars, and a tomb district known as the Tombs of the Kings. It is the sensible base because it has everything: fuel, food, hotels, rental shops. Geroskipou and Chlorakas are smaller towns just along the coast where the pace is quieter and the bakeries are good. Come to Paphos for the practical side and to see the mosaic floors, then leave in the morning.

The road to Kouklia is the old coastal route towards Limassol, with fields of bananas and greenhouses squeezed against the sea on one side and dry hills on the other. The surface is generally good, the corners are open, and the real hazards are tour buses, rental cars driven by people who are still working out which side of the road to use, and the fact that traffic keeps left, a leftover of British rule. In summer the heat is fierce by noon, and the light is hard, so early or late rides make more sense. Spring is lovely, with wildflowers on the verges and green slopes.

At Kouklia the medieval manor house stands over the ruins, a Lusignan-era building later used as a sugar estate, and a small museum holds finds from the sanctuary. The stone known as the Cone of Aphrodite, a conical black block, is associated with the cult, and that is the most interesting thing you can look at. From here the island opens eastward, towards Choirokoitia and the Neolithic village on the hill, which is one of the oldest settlement sites in the Mediterranean.
t.memphis and its necropolis the pyramid f:
This is Giza and the great Old Kingdom necropolis, the first place on any list of Egypt, and a hard one to write about without sounding like a postcard. Memphis was the capital of the early pharaohs, on the Nile just south of modern Cairo, and the pyramid fields stretch along the desert edge from Giza down through Saqqara and Dahshur. The Great Pyramid was built for Khufu around 2560 BC and was the tallest man-made structure on earth for several thousand years. The sheer age is the thing that gets you: when the Greeks and Romans visited as tourists, these were already ancient.

The landscape is a limestone plateau on the western bank, with the green strip of the Nile valley to the east and the open Sahara beyond. Light is best at dawn, when the plateau is cool and the pyramids glow, or at sunset, when the haze softens them. In summer the heat is fierce by mid-morning, and shade is scarce, so carry plenty of water and a hat.

Riding here is a different game. Cairo's traffic is dense and fast, with little respect for lanes, and the road to the plateau is lined with touts, horses and camel drivers who will approach you the moment you stop. A firm, friendly no works. Check with the ticket office about where bikes may be parked, and keep valuables locked. If you are bringing your own bike to Egypt, customs paperwork and a carnet need careful planning well in advance.

Fuel is easy in the Cairo area, which has several million people, and the city around the pyramids offers plenty of cafes. The older Islamic necropoles of Cairo, like the ones named for Imam al-Shafi'i and Sayyida Nafisa, form a vast City of the Dead where people really live among the tombs, and they make a fascinating and very different contrast to the pyramids.
t.aphrodite s sacred city at kato paphos t:
Aphrodite was born from the sea foam off this coast, according to the Greeks, and the oldest part of her story is a few kilometres east of Paphos, at a sea stack called Petra tou Romiou and at the sanctuary of Palaepaphos in the village of Kouklia. But the city of Nea Paphos, the new Paphos, which grew by the harbour at Kato Paphos, was where the island's rulers lived. Founded at the end of the fourth century BC, it became the capital of Cyprus under the Ptolemies and then the Romans, and it stayed that way until the fourth century AD. UNESCO listed Paphos in 1980 as a site of remarkable archaeological remains.

The archaeological park by the harbour holds the best of it: Roman villas with floors covered in mosaics of dazzling colour and quality, showing scenes from Greek myth, Dionysus and his followers, Theseus and the Minotaur, Aion and Apollo, all in tiny cubes of stone laid in the third and fourth centuries AD. The Odeon, a small Roman theatre, is still used for concerts. A little further inland, the Tombs of the Kings, carved into the rock, are not royal at all, but belonged to high officials, and are impressive. Paphos Castle, a small fort at the harbour mouth, was rebuilt by the Ottomans in the sixteenth century, and the ruined fortress of Saranta Kolones, forty columns, is a relic of the crusader age.

Paphos is a town of about thirty-six thousand people with fuel, food and an international airport, popular with tourists, so the harbour area can feel busy. Remember that Cyprus drives on the left, a legacy of British rule. The riding is lovely. The coast road runs between citrus groves and banana plantations, and inland the road climbs into the Troodos mountains, up to Mount Olympus at 1,952 metres, through pine forest, with villages, monasteries and cool air. Roads are well surfaced but twisty, and hairpins demand care.

Summers are hot, often above thirty-five degrees, so ride in spring, from March to May, when wildflowers cover the hills, or in autumn. Winter can be wet, and snow falls on the Troodos.

Try halloumi grilled, souvlaki and a glass of commandaria, the sweet dessert wine that Cyprus has made for centuries.
t.al imam ash shaf i necropolis@30.0,31.3:
Cairo has a second city that most visitors never think about, a long ribbon of tombs on the southern flank of the old town known as the Qarafa, or City of the Dead. Families live in some of the funerary courtyards, there are shops and bakeries between the mausoleums, and in the middle of it all stands the tomb of Imam al-Shafi'i, the scholar who founded one of the four great schools of Sunni law and died in Egypt in 820. The big domed mausoleum you see today was raised in 1211 by the Ayyubid sultan al-Kamil, and the dome carries a bronze boat-shaped ornament on top that you can spot from surprising distances.

Riding here is an exercise in patience rather than pleasure. The streets around the necropolis are narrow, the surface changes without warning, and the traffic follows its own grammar of horns, nudges and eye contact. Speed is irrelevant; awareness is everything. Go early, ideally just after sunrise on a Friday, when the city is quieter and the light comes low and gold across the domes. Midday in summer is brutal, with heat bouncing off limestone and dust in your teeth.

Fuel is no problem, since you are inside a metropolis of many millions, with Giza only a few kilometres to the west and the centre of Cairo not much further. Park where someone you can see is watching the bikes, and ask before wandering into the courtyards, because they are both sacred ground and, for some, a front garden.

From here the rides head south toward the ruins of ancient Memphis, the first capital of a united Egypt, and the pyramid fields of Saqqara and Giza. That is the pleasure of this start: within an hour the tomb-city gives way to canals, palm groves and farmland along the Nile, with the pyramids of different eras standing on the desert edge like a family portrait spanning two thousand years. Carry water, cover your shoulders when entering the shrine, and leave your helmet at the door with someone who looks reliable.
t.sabie@-25.1,30.8:
Sabie is a forestry town in the hills of Mpumalanga, where the Lowveld climbs into the Drakensberg escarpment and mist rolls through the pine plantations almost every morning. The surrounding area holds one of the largest man-made forests in the world, planted over the last century with pine and eucalyptus, and the sweet resin smell lingers in the air. Water pours off the escarpment everywhere, and the town is the base for a string of waterfalls: Mac Mac, Lone Creek, Bridal Veil and Horseshoe all lie within a short ride.

Long Tom Pass climbs out of Sabie toward Lydenburg and tops out at about 2,150 metres, one of the highest roads in the province. It takes its name from the big Boer artillery guns, called Long Toms, that were hauled up here during the Anglo-Boer War, and a replica gun stands at the summit. The road is a delight, with long, smooth bends and fast sweepers through pine forest and open grassland, and good views back toward the Lowveld on clear days. Mist and rain are common, and the road can be wet and slick, so go carefully.

The history of the area is tied to gold. Prospectors poured in during the 1870s, and Pilgrim's Rest, a short ride north, was the heart of the rush and is now a living museum of tin-roofed houses. Sabie has a more peaceful air today, with trout fishing in the streams, craft shops and a few cafes, and the Panorama Route begins just to the north, leading on to Blyde River Canyon.

Sabie has fuel, food and plenty of places to stay, and larger towns lie within an hour, with Lydenburg about thirty-four kilometres away and White River the same distance in the other direction. The best time is autumn and winter, when the days are dry and clear, though mornings are cold. Summer brings heavy afternoon thunderstorms. Watch out for loose gravel on the bends, and for slow lorries carrying timber.
t.thunder bay@48.4,-89.2:
Thunder Bay is the end of the line for the Ontario shore of Lake Superior, a port city of just under a hundred thousand people tucked against a huge bay with the long, flat shape of Sleeping Giant rising across the water. That peninsula, a cluster of cliffs and ridges, gives the city's skyline a nearly mythic profile, and the Ojibwe story says it is Nanabijou, the spirit of the deep sea, turned to stone. The name of the city comes from the bay, and the weather justifies it: storms off the lake can be sudden and loud.

For more than a century Thunder Bay was the point where the grain of the Canadian prairies met the ships. The big concrete elevators along the waterfront once loaded vast amounts of wheat for export through the Great Lakes, and the city's twin origins, in Fort William, which began as a fur-trade post of the North West Company, and Port Arthur, which grew as a railway terminus, still show in its two distinct downtowns. Old Fort William, a reconstruction of the fur-trade depot, is open in summer with costumed interpreters.

The ride along the north shore, from Sault Ste. Marie on Highway 17, is the reason to arrive here, and it is a fine one, mostly empty and mostly wooded, with the lake appearing and disappearing through the spruce. By the time you reach Thunder Bay you will have covered something like seven hundred kilometres of road with few towns, so the sight of a large city with a proper supermarket is a relief. Fuel, repairs, restaurants and motels are all easy here, which makes it the obvious place to rest.

The weather is the main uncertainty. Lake Superior makes its own climate, and fog, cold winds and sudden rain are normal even in summer, with the cold water chilling the air along the shore. Pack warm layers, and expect mosquitoes and black flies in early summer. The cliffs of Kakabeka Falls, a short ride west, are worth the stop, with a thundering waterfall sometimes called the Niagara of the North.

Try a Persian, a local pastry covered with pink icing, a Thunder Bay peculiarity that people take surprisingly seriously.
t.houghton@47.1,-88.6:
Houghton sits on the Keweenaw Peninsula, a thumb of land that pokes into Lake Superior so far north that it feels like another country. Here the Portage Canal slices the peninsula in two, and the town and its twin, Hancock, face each other across the water, joined by a double-decked lift bridge whose road deck rises to let boats pass beneath. The twin hillside towns, with their brick storefronts and steep streets, look like an overgrown mining camp, and that is what they were.

Copper made the place. Long before Europeans arrived, Native people mined nuggets of pure copper from the rocks here, and in the 1840s a rush brought thousands of immigrants, Cornish, Finnish, Italian and many more, to dig the richest native copper deposits in the world. The mines ran for a century, and their head-frames and stone ruins still dot the hills. In Hancock, the Quincy Mine's great hoist house is open for tours, and you can ride a cog railway and go underground. The Cornish brought the pasty, a meat-and-vegetable turnover that is the local lunch, and the Finns left their saunas and their surnames.

Michigan Technological University, founded to train mining engineers, keeps the town young and gives it a few good coffee shops. Winter here is serious: the peninsula gets some of the heaviest snowfall in the eastern United States, often over two hundred inches in a season, and the banks beside the roads can stand taller than a car. So riding is a summer and early autumn affair. US 41 runs north from town to Copper Harbor at the tip, climbing and falling through hardwood forest, and Brockway Mountain Drive, a ridge road built in the 1930s, gives a huge view over the lake.

Houghton has fuel, supermarkets, diners and motels, and north of it services thin out, so top the tank here. Expect lake-effect fog and sudden chill, even in July, as Superior is cold enough to cool the whole peninsula. Early autumn is the best time, with crisp days and color arriving in late September, while black flies can be fierce in late spring. The great lake itself, with its rocky shore and agate-strewn beaches, is the real destination, and the cold, clear water is a pleasure to stand beside.
t.egg harbor@45.1,-87.3:
Egg Harbor is the first village of Door County that makes you stop, and it has a name with a story to match. The legend says that in the 1860s a group of boaters returning from a trip to Green Bay got into a fight over a basket of eggs, throwing them at one another until the boat was thoroughly and unmistakably scrambled. Whether or not that is true, the name stuck, and it suits a place that tends to be more playful than solemn.

The peninsula is a narrow finger of limestone separating the waters of Green Bay from Lake Michigan, and Egg Harbor sits on the bay side, where the shore is gentle and the sunsets face west across the water. Cherry and apple orchards line the roads nearby, and in May the blossom is thick enough to turn a hillside white. The cherries are harvested in July, and roadside stands sell them fresh, dried, and baked into pies. Vineyards and small wineries have joined the orchards, and the smell of ripe fruit and cut grass drifts through the open visor.

Highway 42 is the road, and it is a pleasant ride rather than a technical one. It runs along the bay shore, through small villages, with bends that are gentle and visibility that is generous. The speed limit drops in town, and traffic can be heavy in July and August, especially on weekends, so mid-week mornings or autumn days are better. The shoulders are narrow, and cyclists are plentiful, so keep your distance. Fog off the lake can roll in, and the temperature can change quickly across the peninsula.

For fuel, the safe plan is to fill in Sturgeon Bay, about twenty-five kilometres south, before heading up the peninsula, though small stations are scattered along the way. Egg Harbor itself has plenty of places to eat, from bakeries to casual restaurants, and a fish boil, a Door County tradition in which whitefish and potatoes are boiled in a huge kettle over an open fire, is the thing to try if your timing allows. Autumn colour comes in October and is excellent. Winter is quiet, with many places closed, and ice can make the roads tricky.
t.fish creek@45.1,-87.2:
Fish Creek feels like the postcard version of Door County, and it has the good sense to wear it lightly. The village sits on the shore of Green Bay at the edge of Peninsula State Park, its main street lined with old frame buildings, galleries, and cafes, while the harbour is dotted with boats. It was settled in the mid-nineteenth century by Alexander Noble, a pioneer who built a pier and a mill, and the town grew up around the needs of lake traffic and lumbering.

The state park next door is the real prize. Peninsula State Park covers thousands of acres of limestone bluff, forest, and shoreline, with the Niagara Escarpment, the same ridge that creates Niagara Falls, forming steep cliffs at the water's edge. A road winds around the park, with views over the bay, and the Eagle Bluff Lighthouse, built in 1868, stands on the cliff top. Birdlife is plentiful, and the water is clear and cold. Fish Creek also has a long-running outdoor theatre in the woods, founded in the 1930s, which draws audiences each summer.

The riding is gentle and scenic. Highway 42 runs through the village, and the road to the park is narrow and winding, with trees arching overhead. It is slow going, with low speed limits and a lot of pedestrians in the summer. The best time is early morning or after the crowds thin out, in September or October, when the maples and birches turn and the light over the water is soft. Be careful of deer, which wander onto the road at dusk, and of wet leaves in autumn.

Fish Creek has plenty of food, from bakeries to restaurants, and a fish boil is again a local tradition to try. Fuel is less certain, and it is safest to fill in Sturgeon Bay before heading north, as the larger towns on the mainland, such as Menominee across the bay, are far enough away to matter. In winter, the village goes quiet, and many shops close, but the park stays open for snowshoeing and skiing. Take a jacket, whatever the season, because the breeze off the bay can be cool even on a warm afternoon.
t.sister bay@45.2,-87.1:
Sister Bay is the northern anchor of Door County's bay shore, and it wears its Scandinavian heritage with a certain amount of humour. Norwegians, Swedes, and Danes settled this part of Wisconsin in the nineteenth century, drawn by the fishing and the timber, and you can still see their influence in the names, the food, and the architecture. The most famous example is a restaurant with a sod roof on which goats graze all summer, a sight that makes most riders pull over and take a picture before they quite know why.

The village sits in a sheltered bay, with a marina and a waterfront park, and the bluffs rise behind it. It is the last decent-sized settlement before the peninsula narrows toward its tip, and the roads fan out toward Ellison Bay and Gills Rock. From Gills Rock or nearby Northport, a ferry crosses to Washington Island, through a passage that French explorers named Porte des Morts, or Death's Door, because of the shipwrecks that the strong currents and storms caused. The crossing is short and ordinary now, but the name remains.

Highway 42 is again the road, and north of Sister Bay it becomes quieter and more rural, with farms and woods and occasional glimpses of the lake. The corners are gentle, and the ride is relaxed, though the shoulders are narrow and the summer traffic can be slow. In autumn the trees turn to gold and red, and the roads empty. Fog and sudden rain are possible on the peninsula, and the temperature can be much lower near the water than inland, so keep a layer in the pannier.

Sister Bay has a good selection of cafes, bakeries, and restaurants, and the cherry products are as good here as anywhere. Fuel is available in the larger villages on the peninsula, but the sensible reference point for a full tank is Sturgeon Bay, or Menominee on the far shore, both a fair distance away. In winter, the village is quiet and the water often freezes at the edges. A hot drink by the harbour, with the wind coming across the bay, is a fine way to end a long day on the road.
t.gills rock@45.3,-87.0:
Gills Rock sits at the end of the line on Door County's northern tip, a tiny fishing village of a few houses, a maritime museum, and a harbour full of working boats. The road that has carried you up the peninsula finally runs out of room here, with Green Bay on one side and the strait beyond. That strait has a name that sells itself: Porte des Morts, or Death's Door, a stretch of water between the peninsula and Washington Island where shifting currents, shoals and sudden storms have wrecked a long list of ships. Whether the French or the Potawatomi named it is debated, but the reputation is earned.

The village was settled by Scandinavians in the nineteenth century, and the fishing tradition continues. Whitefish and trout come off the boats, and a fish boil or smoked fish is the right thing to eat. The Door County Maritime Museum has a branch here, with old fishing tugs, engines and charts, and it gives a good picture of what working these waters meant. You can usually watch the boats come in, and in the evening the whole harbour glows.

The riding to get here is a pleasure. State Highway 42 runs up the Green Bay side of the peninsula through orchards, small harbour towns and woods, with views over the water through gaps in the trees. It is a quiet, slow road with gentle bends, and in the north it narrows and becomes more rural. Watch for deer, cyclists, and the odd tractor, and keep your speed down through the villages. Spring and early summer bring cherry blossom, and autumn brings the colour, but the best season for solitude is late September or early June. In midsummer the road is packed with sightseeing cars.

Both towns also have places to eat and a bed for the night. If you want to cross to Washington Island, a ferry runs from nearby Northport, and the trip takes about half an hour.

Take a minute at the shore. On a still day the strait looks harmless. It never is.
t.ola@59.6,151.3:
Ola is a fishing town of a little over six thousand people on the northern shore of the Sea of Okhotsk, about twenty-eight kilometres east of Magadan. It sits where the Ola River runs into a lagoon, behind a long sandy spit, and the surrounding country is a mix of low hills, larch forest and wide marsh. The climate is hard, with cold, dry winters and cool, foggy summers, because the sea stays icy well into spring and chills the coast.

The road from Magadan is an easy and pleasant ride by Kolyma standards. The surface is generally good asphalt, with gentle bends and light traffic, and the views open over the coast and the hills as you leave the city. In summer the roadside is a mass of wildflowers, with fireweed and dwarf birch, and in autumn the larch turns a rich gold. Fog is the main hazard, rolling in from the sea and reducing visibility, and winter brings ice, snow and strong winds that can make riding impractical. June to September is the sensible season.

Ola has fuel, shops and cafes, though the range is modest, and Magadan, with some ninety-five thousand people, is the place for anything more serious. The main business here has always been fish, and in summer and autumn the salmon runs bring a flurry of activity to the river and the lagoon. Try the fish soup, smoked salmon or dried fish at a local stall, and if you are lucky, a spoonful of red caviar on bread, which is a Far Eastern habit and deserves your attention.

Nature is the great attraction. The lagoon and the coast are rich in birds, from gulls and terns to ducks and waders, and in spring and autumn they gather in large numbers. Brown bears wander along the shore in salmon season, so keep a distance and never leave food in your tent. The spit shelters a long, quiet beach where the water is cold and clear, and the sky often turns pale gold at dusk. It is a place to slow down, listen to the surf and breathe in salt air before the road takes you back to town.
t.white city of tel aviv the modern moveme:
White walls, rounded balconies, ribbon windows and flat roofs: walking through central Tel Aviv you are surrounded by one of the largest collections of buildings in the International Style anywhere in the world. Several thousand were built in the 1930s and 1940s, many by architects who had trained in Europe, some at the Bauhaus, and who adapted the modernist ideas to the Mediterranean climate with balconies for shade and raised ground floors for air. The White City, as it is called, became a World Heritage Site in 2003. The plan of the city itself was drawn up by the Scottish urbanist Patrick Geddes in the 1920s, with tree lined boulevards and green squares.

Rothschild Boulevard, with its central promenade of trees, kiosks and cafés, is the heart of the White City, and Bialik Street and the area around Dizengoff Square are full of fine examples. The Bauhaus Center on Dizengoff organises walking tours, and many buildings have been restored, though others are still waiting.

Tel Aviv is a lively, modern city on the beach, with a long promenade, cafés, bars and a strong nightlife. Jaffa, the old port town to the south, has a historic core, a flea market and excellent restaurants. The city is relaxed and informal, and the beaches are packed on summer weekends.

Riding in Tel Aviv is urban riding, with heavy traffic, scooters and electric bikes everywhere, and aggressive driving. Parking a motorcycle is relatively easy, on pavements in designated areas. On the Sabbath, from Friday evening to Saturday evening, public transport stops and the city is quieter. Summer is hot and humid; spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Fuel and services are everywhere. Food in Tel Aviv is excellent and varied: try sabich, hummus, shakshuka and the fresh produce of the Carmel market. Check the current security situation and travel advice before visiting.
t.aphrodite s sanctuary at kouklia village:
According to the Greeks, Aphrodite rose from the sea foam off the coast of Cyprus, and the place where she came ashore was near Paphos. The rock of Petra tou Romiou, a sea stack a few kilometres east of Kouklia, is the traditional spot, and the sanctuary on the hill above, at Palaepaphos, was one of the most important shrines of the ancient world. People came on pilgrimage from across the Mediterranean from the Bronze Age to late antiquity, and the cult went back to a Near Eastern fertility goddess long before the Greeks arrived, with the goddess worshipped in the form of a cone-shaped black stone.

The sanctuary was rebuilt many times, and in the Middle Ages the Lusignan kings built a manor house on the site, using stones from the ancient temple, and this building now houses a museum with the sacred stone and finds from the excavations. The site was included in UNESCO's listing of Paphos in 1980. The ruins are modest, a series of walls and foundations on a ridge, but the setting is open, with a view over the sea, and the story is vivid.

The ride is straightforward. Cyprus, like Britain, drives on the left, a legacy of British rule, and the roads are generally good, with a fast coastal highway between Limassol and Paphos, past beaches, banana plantations and the Petra tou Romiou. Inland, the roads climb into the Troodos mountains, with pine forest, small villages and cooler air, reaching nearly two thousand metres at Mount Olympus. Winding routes up from the coast give excellent riding, with hairpins and views, but surfaces can be rough, and summer traffic is heavy. In July and August the heat is intense, so spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Fuel is available in Paphos and the larger villages along the coast, and the area is full of cafes and tavernas, serving halloumi, grilled meat and the local sweet wine, Commandaria. Take water and sun protection, because the site has little shade, and try to arrive early or late in the day. If you stop at Petra tou Romiou, take care crossing the road, since it is busy and the car park can be crowded.
t.kato paphos necropolis@34.8,32.4:
The so-called Tombs of the Kings lie on the sea edge of Paphos, in the western corner of Cyprus, and the name is a bit of romance, because nobody royal was ever proven to be buried here. In fact the rock-cut tombs date to the Hellenistic and Roman periods, roughly the fourth century BC onward, and they were used by the high officials and wealthy citizens of Nea Paphos, the old capital of the island under the Ptolemies. The tombs are carved into the soft limestone, some with Doric columns around a central open court, so that you walk down a flight of steps into what looks like a sunken Greek house with a burial chamber on each side.

Early Christians sheltered in some of them as well, and the grounds feel a bit like a stony park, with caper bushes, wild thyme and fennel growing from the cracks and the sea sounding close behind. The site is part of the wider UNESCO area of Paphos, which also includes the mosaic floors of the Roman villas and the harbour fort, all within a short walk or ride.

Riding around Paphos is easy, with flat coastal roads, roundabouts and a lot of tourist traffic in summer. Beyond the town the landscape rises quickly toward the Troodos, and the road to Polis or toward the hills offers real bends, vineyards and old villages. Do keep an eye out for rental cars, which are driven on the left in Cyprus, an inheritance from the British, and for sand and gravel on the shoulders. Midday in July and August is hot enough that you will want to stop in the shade, so go early, or in the late afternoon for the better light on the stone.

Paphos has all the services you would want, with plenty of fuel stations along the main roads, good cafés and a long line of fish tavernas by the harbour. Chlórakas and Emba, both a few kilometres away, are also substantial villages with shops and fuel. The site has an entry fee and sets modest hours that are shorter in winter, so check ahead if you are arriving late. Wear shoes with grip, since the rock steps are worn, and bring water, as there is little shade among the tombs.
t.neys provincial park@48.8,-86.6:
Ney's Provincial Park holds one of the quieter chapters of Canadian history. During the Second World War, a camp here held German prisoners of war, and visitors can still learn something about it at the site. Today the park is a pleasant place, with a long sand beach on Lake Superior, dunes, a rock headland with a lookout, and a campground in the trees, all within a few kilometres of the town of Marathon.

Marathon, with about three thousand people, is the nearest place for fuel, food and supplies. It was a pulp mill town founded in the 1940s and still has an industrial feel, but it has the pumps and groceries, which is what matters. The Trans-Canada Highway runs through here, and the riding between Wawa and Marathon is among the finest on the north shore: long rolling hills, glimpses of the lake, rock cuttings and the smell of spruce and cold water.

The lake is the main character. Superior is deep, clear and cold, and the sand here is fine, with driftwood piled in lines along the beach. On a calm morning, with the mist rising off the water, it is easy to stand on the headland for longer than you meant to. The park lies on the Canadian Shield, some of the oldest rock on the continent, and the shoreline shows its polished boulders and glacial scours.

Plan for weather. The lake can cool the air by many degrees, fog sometimes drifts in on warm days, and storms can arrive from nowhere. Summer is short, from about June to September, and the park is quiet outside that time. Mosquitoes and black flies can be fierce in early summer, so bring repellent. For a night stop, the campground is lovely, and Marathon has a small number of motels if you want a bed.
t.ekkeroy@70.1,30.1:
Ekkerøy is a small peninsula sticking out into the Varangerfjord, joined to the mainland by a narrow causeway, and it is one of the best places in the Arctic to watch seabirds from the road. Thousands of kittiwakes nest on the cliffs in summer, packed on every ledge, and the noise and smell are overwhelming in the best way. The birds wheel and shriek and drop off the cliff in clouds, and on a calm day you can sit with a sandwich and watch for as long as you like. Eider ducks, shags and gulls share the shore, and out on the water you may see more.

The village itself is a handful of old wooden houses, a white wooden church and a tiny harbour, set in a landscape of bare rock, grass and driftwood. People fished here for generations, and the houses once held far more families than they do now. The rock formations along the shore are unusual, with strange, weathered shapes of grey stone and pale sand, and in the low light of evening they seem to glow. There are paths to walk, but nothing difficult, and the whole peninsula can be seen in an hour or two.

The road is a short, quiet side road off the main route, about fourteen kilometres from Vadsø, with a good surface and gentle bends. In summer it is easy riding, with only the odd campervan and a few walkers. The wind can be fierce, and you will want a windproof layer, because the temperature on the point is often several degrees lower than in town. Midnight sun brings long evenings when the light on the cliffs turns gold, and it is a magical time to be here. In winter the place is dark, cold and nearly empty.

Kirkenes, further east, is the other town in the region, but it is a long way. A flask and a packed lunch are all you need, since the peninsula has few services, although a small café or museum may be open in summer. Take binoculars if you have them, and leave nesting birds well alone, for the colony is easily disturbed.
t.tel aviv@32.1,34.8:
Tel Aviv is a city that is barely more than a century old. It was founded in 1909 on the sand dunes north of the old port of Jaffa by a group of Jewish families, and it grew with astonishing speed. In the 1930s, architects who had trained in Germany and in the Bauhaus tradition built thousands of modernist apartment blocks, with white walls, curved balconies and small windows to keep out the sun, and the White City is now listed by UNESCO as a remarkable example of that style. Rothschild Boulevard, lined with trees and cafes, is the best place to see them.

The pace of life is quick and the climate is warm and humid for most of the year, with the beach the centre of social life. A promenade runs along the coast, and the sunsets are famous. Jaffa, to the south, is far older, a port of stone lanes and a clock tower, where the sea has been a gateway for three thousand years. Food is a highlight, from hummus and fresh falafel to seafood and market stalls at the Carmel Market.

For a rider, Tel Aviv's roads are fast and demanding, with heavy traffic on the Ayalon highway and a lot of scooters. Parking for two wheels is usually easy. The afternoon ride heads inland and east toward the hills of Judea, where terraced slopes of olive and vine, springs and old stone farming villages make up a cultural landscape of ancient agricultural practice. The land changes quickly from coastal plain to rocky hills, and the temperature drops with height.

Be aware that the region's security situation can change quickly. Check current travel advice and local conditions before setting out, and be prepared for checkpoints and road closures on some routes. Fuel is easy in the city and along the main roads. Shabbat, from Friday evening to Saturday evening, brings quieter streets and fewer shops open in many parts of the country, though Tel Aviv itself is lively throughout. Carry water in summer and wear a helmet and layers.
t.mosque of ahmed ibn tulun@30.0,31.3:
Ibn Tulun is the quiet old-timer of Cairo, a vast mosque built between 876 and 879 by a governor who rose from Turkish slave soldier to master of Egypt and founder of a short-lived dynasty. Ahmad ibn Tulun sent his architects to create something in the style of the Abbasid capital at Samarra in Iraq, and what they made is a huge rectangular courtyard surrounded by arcades of pointed arches in brick and stucco, with carved plaster ornaments that still look sharp after eleven centuries. It is the oldest mosque in Cairo to survive in its original form, and one of the largest in the Islamic world by area.

The minaret is the thing you remember. A spiral staircase winds around the outside of a tower that rises from a square base, in a form that echoes the great spiral minarets of Samarra. The climb is worth every step, since the top gives a view across the courtyard and over the rooftops of the old quarter toward the Citadel. A legend, repeated by guides, says that the mosque was built on the very mountain where Noah's ark came to rest; the story is charming and has no evidence behind it, but the hill on which the mosque stands is indeed a bit higher than the surroundings. A small museum next door, in two joined old houses, is a fine place to see how wealthy Cairenes lived in the Ottoman period.

Riding here, honestly, is an exercise in humility. Cairo is a city of more than seven million, and its streets are crowded with minibuses, tuk-tuks, donkey carts, pedestrians and horns, with lane markings treated as suggestions. If you ride a motorcycle in the city, plan routes with care, avoid the rush hours, and expect to be the smallest thing on the road. Many travellers prefer to leave the bike and take a taxi for the old quarter, where the lanes are narrow and parking is difficult.

Fuel stations are plentiful in the city and cheap by European standards, and the streets around the mosque have small cafes, bakeries and stalls serving tea and fresh bread. The best time to visit is early in the morning or late afternoon, when the light on the brick is warm and the courtyard is calm. Cover your shoulders and knees, and take off your shoes at the door. The air smells of dust, spices and baking bread, and the call to prayer echoes across the rooftops at dusk.
t.as sayyidah nafisah necropolis@30.0,31.3:
South of the Citadel, in the part of Cairo that visitors often skip, lies the Southern Cemetery, a huge area of tombs, mausolea and mosques that has served the city for more than a thousand years. People live here, too, in houses built among the graves, and the area has the feel of a quiet neighbourhood where the dead are simply the oldest residents. The larger complex is often called the City of the Dead, though the name hardly does justice to its busy shops, schoolchildren and washing lines.

Sayyida Nafisa was a great-granddaughter of Hasan, the grandson of the Prophet, and she settled in Egypt in the early ninth century, where she became famous for her piety and learning. She died in 824, and her tomb became a place of pilgrimage that has never stopped drawing visitors. The mosque that stands today was largely rebuilt in later centuries, and it is a busy place on Fridays, when families come to pray and sit in the courtyard. Imam al-Shafi'i, the founder of one of the four main schools of Sunni law, who was a friend of hers, is buried not far away in a famous mausoleum with a wooden boat on top of its dome.

For a motorcyclist, this is an area to approach with caution and respect. The roads are crowded and often rough, with stray animals, children playing and carts, and the traffic pattern is unpredictable. The area around the shrine can be extremely crowded on religious occasions, and photography should be done discreetly, with permission where people are visible. Dress modestly, and ask before entering mosques. The people are generally friendly, and a polite greeting goes a long way.

Fuel and services are available on the main roads toward the Citadel and the Nile, and small cafes serve tea and simple food. The best time to visit is in the morning, before the heat, when the light is soft on the domes and the streets are calm. In summer the heat can be severe, so carry water and take breaks in the shade. The air smells of incense, dust and frying bread. In the evening the lights of the Citadel glow in the distance, and the place has an unforced, human warmth that the grand monuments sometimes lack.
t.qayitbay necropolis@30.0,31.3:
Of all the monuments in Cairo's cemeteries, the funerary complex of the Mamluk sultan Qaitbay is the one that stops people in their tracks. The sultan, who ruled Egypt for nearly thirty years in the later fifteenth century, built it between 1472 and 1474 as a combined mosque, tomb, school and fountain, in the desert fringe east of the city that served as the Mamluk burial ground. What makes it famous is the dome, carved from stone in a continuous pattern of stars and arabesques, so delicate that it looks like lace or a woven carpet rather than masonry. It is regarded as the high point of Mamluk architecture.

The Mamluks were a military caste of slave soldiers, mostly of Turkish and Circassian origin, who ruled Egypt and Syria for more than two and a half centuries, and they spent their wealth on grand buildings, often along the edges of the city. The Northern Cemetery, where Qaitbay's complex stands, is a landscape of domes and minarets among streets and modern housing, and people have lived among the tombs for generations. A walk through it is a fascinating, slightly surreal experience, and the stone domes rise out of ordinary neighbourhoods with children playing football beside them.

Riding in this district requires care. Roads are narrow, often unmarked and shared with pedestrians, handcarts and vehicles of all kinds, and the surface is patchy in places. Cairo traffic as a whole is dense, so allow plenty of time and choose quiet hours, early in the morning or on Fridays, when the streets are calmer. The area is not a place to wander alone with expensive equipment, so keep your belongings close, and consider hiring a local guide who can explain the monuments and smooth the way.

Fuel and food are easy to find on the main roads, and small stalls offer tea, sweet pastries and fresh juice. The inside of the mosque is cool and quiet, and the courtyard is a restful place after the noise of the streets. The best light on the dome is in the late afternoon, when the carved stone glows a warm gold. The smell is of dust, old stone and the smoke of the neighbourhood's bakeries. Even if you stay only twenty minutes, the dome stays in the mind.
t.historic cairo@30.1,31.3:
The heart of medieval Cairo is a dense maze of lanes, domes and minarets that has barely changed in some corners since the Mamluk age, and it is one of the richest collections of Islamic architecture on earth. UNESCO listed Historic Cairo in 1979, recognising hundreds of monuments, mosques, madrasas, baths and gates, built over a thousand years. The city was founded as a royal enclosure by the Fatimid dynasty in 969, and its name, al-Qahira, means the victorious. The Fatimids also founded Al-Azhar, a mosque and teaching institution that has been running since the 970s and is regarded as one of the oldest universities in the world.

The main artery is the street called al-Muizz, a long road lined with monuments from different periods, including mosques, sabils, or public fountains, and old merchants' houses. It leads past two imposing gates, the Bab al-Futuh and the Bab Zuweila, which you can climb for a view over the district. The Khan el-Khalili, a market dating back to the fourteenth century, is nearby, with alleys of spice, lamps, gold and souvenirs. The Citadel of Saladin, founded in the late twelfth century, stands on a rocky spur above the city, with the Ottoman-style mosque of Muhammad Ali dominating the skyline.

For a motorcyclist, the old city is best approached on foot. The lanes are narrow and crowded, there are street vendors, donkey carts and pedestrians everywhere, and motor traffic is restricted in some parts. Ride in early, park at the edge, and walk. The main roads around the district are notoriously congested, with an unceasing flow of horns and minibuses, and a calm temper is your best accessory. Dress modestly, carry small change for tips and tickets, and keep an eye on your belongings in the crowds.

Cairo has fuel stations in every district, and fuel is relatively cheap. The old city has many small cafes where you can sit and watch the bustle over mint tea, and a bowl of koshari, a mix of rice, lentils, pasta and fried onions, is the classic cheap lunch. The air smells of spices, charcoal smoke and dust, and the sound of the call to prayer rises from dozens of minarets at once. The best time to visit is early morning or late afternoon, when the heat eases and the light picks out the carved stone.
t.magadan@59.6,150.8:
Magadan sits on a bay of the Sea of Okhotsk at the end of a very long road, and the sense of being at the end of the world is very strong. The town was founded in the 1930s as the base of Dalstroy, the Soviet agency that ran gold mining and forced labour camps in the Kolyma region, and for the prisoners who were shipped here, Magadan was the gateway to a world of cold and hardship from which many never returned. The scale of the suffering is difficult to take in, and a memorial on a hill above the town, called the Mask of Sorrow, a giant concrete face with tears made of small faces, was designed by the sculptor Ernst Neizvestny and unveiled in 1996.

The city today has about ninety-five thousand people, and a quiet, resilient character. It is a port and a base for gold and silver mining, and its streets, lined with Soviet-era apartment blocks painted in bright colours to combat the grey winters, climb the slopes above the harbour. The sea is cold and the air smells of salt, with gulls over the fish port. A regional museum covers the history of the area, the gold rush and the camp era.

The road that leaves Magadan is the Kolyma Highway, built by prisoners in the 1930s and 1940s and later nicknamed the Road of Bones, after the many who died building it. It runs more than two thousand kilometres to Yakutsk across mountains, rivers and permafrost, one of the most remote roads in the world. It is mostly paved near Magadan but turns into gravel and mud farther on, with long distances between fuel stops, and bridges and river crossings that are sometimes out of use. It needs serious preparation and local knowledge.

For a gentler outing, the road to Ola, along the Okhotsk coast, runs east through hills and small fishing settlements, with views of the sea. In summer, salmon fill the rivers, and the villages smoke and salt the catch. The weather can be foggy and cold even in July.

Fuel and services are in Magadan, and it is wise to fill up before leaving town. Summers are short and cool, with the best weather from July to early September. Winters are dark, long and snowy, with strong winds.
t.pyramid fields from giza to dahshur@30.0:
The pyramids of Giza are the most famous ancient monuments on earth, and they are also, absurdly, right at the end of a city street. The plateau lies on the western edge of Giza, a city of some two and a half million, and the urban sprawl runs right up to the fence. The Great Pyramid, built around 2560 BC for the pharaoh Khufu, was the tallest human structure in the world for nearly four thousand years, and it still takes the breath away, even when the first view comes between a fried-chicken sign and a minibus.

But Giza is only the beginning. To the south, along the edge of the desert, lie the necropolis fields of the Old Kingdom: Abusir, Saqqara and Dahshur. At Saqqara stands the Step Pyramid of Djoser, the first great stone building in the world, designed by the architect Imhotep around 2650 BC. At Dahshur, the pharaoh Sneferu built two pyramids, the Bent Pyramid, with its odd change of angle halfway up, and the Red Pyramid, the first true smooth-sided one, and both are far quieter than Giza, with sometimes only a handful of visitors and the wind.

Riding between them is a meeting of old and new. You travel along canal-side roads, through green farmland, palm groves and villages where donkeys pull carts and children wave, and the desert edge shows as a sudden line of sand at the end of a field. Traffic in the Cairo area is wild, with everyone using the horn and few observing lanes, so ride defensively and watch for potholes and speed bumps with no warning. Start at dawn, before the heat and the crowds.

The nearest big place is Giza, with plenty of fuel, but the road south has fewer stations, and some sites in the area lie in military zones with checkpoints, so carry your passport and permits and be patient. Bring water and a hat, and plan on at least half a day for the southern sites. The sand, the silence and the pyramids standing alone on the skyline are well worth the effort.
t.cairo@30.0,31.2:
Cairo is a city that makes sense of every superlative you have heard about it. With more than seven million people in the city proper and many millions more in the metropolitan area, it is the largest in the Arab world and one of the largest in Africa, and its streets are a river of cars, buses, donkey carts, bicycles and pedestrians, all moving at once to the music of horns.

The Egyptian Museum, a pink neoclassical building on the edge of the square, holds the treasures of the pharaohs, including the contents of Tutankhamun's tomb, though many of its finest pieces are moving to a vast new museum near the pyramids. East of the centre lies Islamic Cairo, a labyrinth of medieval streets, mosques, markets and madrasas that is among the richest historic districts in the world. The Khan el-Khalili bazaar sells everything from spices to lamps, and the smell of coffee and frying falafel fills the air.

Riding a motorbike here is a feat of nerve. Lane markings are decorative, traffic lights are advisory, and the unwritten rules include honking to announce yourself rather than to express anger. Keep your speed down, watch every gap, and never assume that anyone has seen you. Friday mornings are the quietest, when the city sleeps in, and it is the best time to move across town. The Nile bridges can bottleneck badly in the afternoon.

Fuel is not a problem in the capital, with stations all over the city, though queues form at busy times. The best advice for the start of a ride is to leave early and head for the ring road, then out into the desert. A glass of sweet mint tea, a plate of koshari, the national dish of rice, lentils and pasta, and a view of the river at sunset make a worthy start or finish to the day.
t.durban@-29.9,31.0:
Durban is the biggest city on South Africa's east coast and the busiest port in the country, a warm, humid, mixed-up place that feels much closer to the Indian Ocean world than to the Cape. The Zulu name for the area is eThekwini, and the city's mix of Zulu, Indian and British heritage shows everywhere, in the street names, the temples and mosques, and above all the food. Indentured laborers from India arrived from the 1860s to work the sugar plantations, and Durban now has the largest Indian-origin population outside India, which accounts for the bunny chow, a hollowed-out loaf filled with curry, that locals consider their own invention.

The seafront, known as the Golden Mile, runs along a wide beach with a promenade lined with hotels, and in the evening it fills with families and surfers. The Moses Mabhida stadium, with its big arch, dominates the skyline near the beach, and the Victoria Street Market is a good place to buy spices. Mahatma Gandhi lived here for twenty-one years from 1893, developing the ideas of nonviolent protest that he later took to India, and the city has several places that remember him.

The weather is warm to hot all year round. Summers are humid and can bring violent thunderstorms, and winters are mild and dry with clear blue skies. The best time to ride is from April to September, when the air is cooler and drier. Rain can fall hard and fast, making roads slick, and in 2022 floods caused heavy damage in and around the city.

For riders, Durban is a base rather than a ride in itself. The traffic can be heavy, and the highways are fast and busy, but beyond the city the coast road north to Ballito and Salt Rock has gentle curves and views of the sea, and the Valley of a Thousand Hills to the west offers pleasant winding roads through Zulu villages. Care with valuables and sensible parking habits are advisable, as in any big city.

Fuel and food are in plentiful supply, with stations on every main road and every kind of restaurant. Try a curry on the beachfront in the evening, and watch the ships queue off the port.
t.ohlange@-29.7,31.0:
Ohlange sits in the hills of Inanda, north-west of Durban, and in the history of South Africa it carries weight far beyond its modest appearance. This is the site of the Ohlange Institute, founded in 1901 by John Langalibalele Dube, a Zulu educator, newspaper publisher and activist who went on to become the first president of the South African Native National Congress, later the African National Congress. Dube built a school here that taught practical skills alongside academic subjects, on the model of Tuskegee in the United States, and it became a center of African education and political thought.

His grave lies on a hill nearby, and the site has been preserved as a memorial. Ohlange also has a powerful place in the story of democracy. In April 1994, Nelson Mandela cast his vote here in the first multiracial election in South African history, choosing to vote at the school rather than in a city polling station as a way of honoring Dube. A small museum and the simple school buildings tell the story, and the atmosphere is quiet and respectful.

The surrounding area is Inanda, a large, hilly district with a mix of formal and informal housing, and it was also the home of Mahatma Gandhi's Phoenix Settlement, which he founded in 1904 on the nearby land. The two sites are close, and visiting both gives a picture of the intertwined struggles for justice in the early twentieth century. The Phoenix Settlement was damaged during unrest in 1985, and it has since been partly restored as a museum.

For a rider, the ride from Durban is a short run through busy suburbs and then into the green hills, on roads that can be potholed and crowded with minibus taxis. Local knowledge is helpful, and it is wise to go with someone who knows the way, or with a guide arranged through a heritage organization. Avoid riding after dark, keep belongings out of sight when stopped, and check the current situation before going.

Fuel and food are best handled in central Durban or in the larger suburbs, where there are stations and plenty of places to eat. Consider making the visit in the morning, when the light is soft over the hills and the school is at its liveliest.
t.vardo@70.4,31.1:
Vardø is the easternmost town in Norway, on a small island in the Barents Sea, and it is reached by an undersea tunnel, the Vardø tunnel, built in the 1980s. The town has about two thousand people, wooden houses painted in soft colours, a harbour and a fortress. The Vardøhus Fortress, finished in 1738, is the northernmost fortress in the world, and it stands guard over the entrance to the Arctic. The town has been a fishing port for centuries, and in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, it was the site of a terrible witch hunt, in which about ninety people, mostly women, were burned at the stake. A memorial by the artist Louise Bourgeois and the architect Peter Zumthor, called the Steilneset Memorial, stands on the shore, with a long wooden hall lit by one bulb for each victim.

Vardø was also a centre of the Pomor trade with northern Russia, and old trading links with Arkhangelsk shaped the culture. The town was largely destroyed in the Second World War, and rebuilt in the plain style of the time. In the last decades, the fishing industry has shrunk, but the town still feels like a working harbour. Seabirds are abundant, and the nearby Hornøya island is home to thousands of nesting puffins, kittiwakes and guillemots, which you can visit by boat in summer. The air here is salty and clean, with a smell of kelp.

The road to Vardø crosses the tundra along the coast, and the last section passes through the tunnel. The surface is excellent, with long, open views over the sea. Wind is a regular factor, and fog is common in summer, as cold sea meets warm air. Winter is harsh, with snow and storms, and the polar night. In summer, the midnight sun lights the town in gold, and it is a magical time to visit.

Fuel and food are available in Vardø, though choices are limited, and it is a good idea to fill up in Vadsø or Varangerbotn. A few cafes and restaurants serve fresh fish, and king crab is a local delicacy. Staying overnight in the town, in a guesthouse by the harbour, gives you the best sense of the place. This is the end of the road in the east, and a very good one.
t.grand portage@48.0,-89.7:
Grand Portage is the far north-eastern tip of Minnesota, where the highway runs out of country against the Canadian border and the Pigeon River. The name is literal. For more than a century, the French and then the British traders who dominated the fur trade carried their canoes and bales around the impassable rapids and falls of the Pigeon River along an eight-and-a-half-mile trail, which they called the Grand Portage, or great carrying place. In the 1780s the North West Company built a depot on the shore of Lake Superior, where canoes from Montreal met those from the interior, and every summer there was a rendezvous with trading, feasting and bargaining.

The depot has been partly rebuilt as Grand Portage National Monument, with a stockade, a great hall and a canoe warehouse, and rangers in period clothing. The land is part of the Grand Portage Reservation, home to a band of the Ojibwe, whose ancestors were here long before the traders, and who guided and fed the voyageurs. Offshore, Isle Royale lies in the lake, with a ferry running from the harbour in summer.

The North Shore Scenic Drive, Highway 61, brings you here along the edge of Lake Superior, the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area, a cold, deep, steel-blue expanse that is more like a sea. The road runs along cliffs of dark basalt, through forest of birch, spruce and pine, past rivers that plunge into the lake over waterfalls. The curves are gentle, the surface is good, and traffic is light except at summer weekends and in the autumn colour season. Just before the border, the High Falls of the Pigeon River, the highest waterfall in Minnesota, can be reached by a short trail.

Services are limited this far north. Grand Marais, a pretty harbour town about thirty-six miles south-west, has fuel, food and lodging, and it makes sense to fill up there. Bring warm clothing, since the lake keeps the air cold even in July, and fog can roll in from the water. Moose and wolves live in the surrounding forest, and the sight of a moose beside the road is a real hazard at dusk. Keep your passport handy if you plan to cross into Ontario, and expect border formalities.
t.lydenburg@-25.1,30.4:
The name Lydenburg means town of suffering, and there is real history behind it. In the 1840s, Voortrekker families settled at Ohrigstad, in the lowveld, but malaria drove them out, and in 1849 they moved up to higher, healthier ground and founded a new town, which they named in memory of what they had endured. Today Lydenburg sits at around 1,400 metres in the Mpumalanga highveld, a quiet market town of about twenty thousand people, with a wide main street, tree-lined avenues and a feel of farming country, where cattle and timber matter more than tourists.

Its most remarkable treasure is far older. In 1957, a boy found fragments of terracotta heads near the town, and archaeologists later pieced together seven large hollow heads made by Iron Age farmers around fifteen centuries ago, among the oldest known sculptures in southern Africa. Replicas are displayed in the local museum, while the originals are kept elsewhere, and the heads, with their strange, stylised faces, are a reminder that the story of this region began long before the Voortrekkers.

The surroundings are big and open. To the west lie grassy hills, trout streams and the cold uplands around Dullstroom, popular with fly fishermen, and to the east the land drops abruptly over the Drakensberg escarpment toward the lowveld, in a series of passes with spectacular views. The town is the start of the climb on the R37 to Sabie over the Long Tom Pass, one of the highest roads in the province, which makes it a natural place to stop for a meal and to fill the tank before a day in the mountains.
