The weather can be changeable. Summer brings afternoon thunderstorms with hail and lightning, and winter nights are cold, with frost on the grass, though days are generally clear and dry. Mist rolls in on the high ground, so a waterproof layer is a good idea at any time of year. Lydenburg has all the basic services, with fuel stations, workshops, banks and cafés, and a few guesthouses that cater for people passing through. Try the local trout, or a plate of braaied boerewors and pap, the standard fare of the region, and set off early, before the clouds gather over the escarpment.
t.long tom pass@-25.1,30.6:
Anyone who loves old guns has heard of Long Tom. In the Anglo-Boer War of 1900, the Boers dragged a few of these huge French-made siege cannon, with barrels long enough to throw shells across valleys, up and down the escarpment to slow the British advance, and the pass takes its name from them. A replica gun stands beside the road near the summit, pointing out over the hills, and it is worth a pause and a photograph before you carry on.

The pass, at roughly 2,150 metres, is one of the highest in Mpumalanga, and it carries the R37 between Lydenburg on the highveld and Sabie in the green hills below. Before the road it was an ox-wagon trail, used by traders hauling goods to the coast at Delagoa Bay, and later by prospectors heading for the goldfields of Pilgrim's Rest. The climb out of Lydenburg is long and gradual, across open grassland, then the road rolls over the top and starts down in a series of bends and curves, with views of misty valleys, rock faces and plantations of pine and eucalyptus.

The weather is the main character. Fog and drizzle are common on the escarpment, particularly in the afternoons, and can reduce visibility to almost nothing, so go slowly and use your lights. In summer, thunderstorms roll in with hail and sudden downpours, while winter mornings can be cold and frosty, with ice in the shade. The best time to ride is a clear morning in autumn, when the air is crisp and the colours of the hillsides are rich. The road surface is good, though some patches deteriorate after storms, and timber lorries use the route all year, so expect slow traffic on the climb.

Around the summit there are no services, so be sure to start with a full tank. Lydenburg, seventeen kilometres away, is the nearest town and has fuel and food, while Sabie, on the other side of the descent, is a small tourist town with cafés, waterfalls and craft shops. Pilgrim's Rest, a preserved gold-rush village, is a short ride beyond, and the whole region is a rewarding place for a few days on a bike. Bring a warm layer for the top, even if it is sunny at the bottom.
t.nottingham road@-29.3,30.0:
Nottingham Road is a village in the middle of the KwaZulu-Natal Midlands that is better known for its pubs and potteries than for its size. It is a stop on the Midlands Meander, a loose trail of craft studios, cheese makers, breweries and restaurants spread over rolling green country, and the place has a relaxed, slightly bohemian atmosphere. Misty mornings are common, with dairy herds in the fields and the Drakensberg a faint blue line on the western horizon.

The history of the region is a mix of colonial farming and the older story of the Zulu kingdom. Near Howick, a short drive away, a small monument marks the spot where Nelson Mandela was arrested in August 1962 while posing as a chauffeur, and a modern sculpture of steel columns that line up to form his face when viewed from the right place now stands there. Visitors can walk the path and view the artwork, and it is an affecting thing to see, set among the fields.

The riding in the Midlands is a pleasure, with gentle hills, long bends and avenues of trees, and country roads that pass farm stalls, trout dams and little villages. The N3, the main highway between Durban and Johannesburg, runs close by and carries heavy lorries, so seek out the quieter back roads when you can. Mist and drizzle are common, particularly in the afternoons, and in summer storms can arrive suddenly, with hail. Winters are crisp, with frost on the grass, and now and then a light dusting of snow on the high ground.

For fuel, Mooi River, about sixteen kilometres away, is a sensible choice, with a population of around ten thousand and the usual services, and Howick, further south-east, is bigger still. The village itself has a few craft shops, cafés and a brewery with a pub, which is worth a lunchtime stop if you are not riding on afterward. The surrounding area has numerous bed and breakfasts and farm cottages, and booking ahead is wise on weekends. Take a layer for the evening, when mist and chill settle on the hills.
t.door county coastal byway point 2@45.1,-:
Egg Harbor is a small, tidy village on the bay side of the peninsula, with a marina, a main street of low wooden buildings and the quiet air of a place that exists mostly for visitors. The name has a story attached to it that locals love to repeat: in the early nineteenth century, crews from two boats supposedly began pelting each other with eggs while waiting at the harbour, and the nickname stuck. Whether or not it is true, it is the kind of tale that makes a place memorable.

The surroundings are the real draw. This part of Door County is orchard country, with rows of cherry and apple trees running down toward the water and small wineries making fruit wines and a few grape varieties. The bay of Green Bay, to the west, is sheltered and quiet, and the sunsets across it are famous. If you stay until evening, the sky over the water turns a deep orange, and the boats in the harbour sit still on the surface.

On the bike, the roads on this side of the peninsula are at their best. Highway 42 is the main road, but side roads curve between orchards and woodland, past farm stands and small barns. The surface is generally good, the corners are gentle, and the speed limits are low, which suits the scenery. Spring brings blossom and cold wind, summer brings heavy traffic and a lot of bicycles, and autumn is when the colours peak, which means the busiest weekends of the year.

Fuel and food are limited in the village itself, though there are a couple of cafes and small restaurants, so top up in Sturgeon Bay, about twenty-five kilometres south. Alternatively, there are petrol stations in some of the larger villages north of here, but they close earlier than you might expect, so do not rely on them late in the evening.

The best time to arrive is mid-morning, after the early fog has lifted and before the crowds arrive. A short walk to the harbour is enough to feel the spirit of the place, with its gulls and sailboats and the smell of cut grass from the orchards. If you are lucky, a stand will be selling cherry pies or a jar of local jam, and that will do for lunch.
t.door county coastal byway point 3@45.1,-:
Fish Creek is the heart of the peninsula's summer life. It sits on the edge of Green Bay at the entrance to Peninsula State Park, one of Wisconsin's best loved parks, and its lanes of wooden shops, galleries and small hotels are busy from June to October. Alexander Noble, who settled here in the 1850s, built a dock and a business around the harbour, and his name remains attached to the village's most historic house.

Peninsula State Park is the draw. It covers thousands of acres of limestone bluffs, forest and shoreline, with a scenic drive that winds through the woods and up to Eagle Bluff Lighthouse, a handsome white building from the 1860s that stands above the water. The park's cliffs drop almost vertically to the bay, and from the observation tower the view takes in islands and distant shores. A few minutes south of the village is one of the oldest professional summer theatres in the country, the Peninsula Players, which performs in a garden setting among the trees.

For the rider, this is the one place on the peninsula where you will want to leave the bike for a while. The park road is slow, with a low speed limit and a lot of cyclists, but it is lovely, passing cedars and birches and, in autumn, flaring maples. Outside the park, Highway 42 runs through the village and can be congested in summer. The best way to enjoy it is to come early or late in the day and let the traffic go by.

Services are fair: there are shops, restaurants and a couple of small stores, but fuel is limited, so top up before you come. Sturgeon Bay, about thirty kilometres south, is the dependable base for anything bigger.

Door County has a tradition of the fish boil, in which whitefish and potatoes are cooked in a big kettle over a wood fire, and the cook throws kerosene on the flames at the end to make the pot boil over and carry away the oil. It is a theatrical performance as well as a meal, and Fish Creek is one of the best places to see it. Even if you do not stay for dinner, you will smell the wood smoke drifting through the village on a summer evening.
t.door county coastal byway point 4@45.2,-:
Sister Bay is best known for its goats. On the roof of a Swedish restaurant on the main street, a small herd of goats grazes on real turf, a tradition that has become a roadside attraction in its own right. It is quirky and charming, and a great way to get a smile out of a cold, tired rider. The village itself, a few hundred metres of shops and cafes on the bay, has a strong Scandinavian flavour, a reminder of the Norwegian, Swedish and Icelandic immigrants who settled in this part of Wisconsin in the nineteenth century.

The harbour is a lively place in summer, with a marina and a small beach, and the bluff above has views across the water to the far shore. The Scandinavian influence extends to the food, with pancakes, meatballs and rye bread on the menus, and a bakery that sells cherry-filled pastries. The long evenings, when the sun lingers over the bay, are a good time to sit outside with a coffee.

For a rider, Sister Bay has the practical edge. It is the largest village in the northern half of the peninsula and has a supermarket, a petrol station and several restaurants, making it a convenient place to take stock before the quieter roads further north. From here, Highway 42 continues up the western shore with some gentle curves and a gradual change in scenery: the farmland gives way to forest, and the road narrows.

The surrounding country is quieter than the area around Fish Creek, partly because the villages are smaller and the roads more winding. If you have time, the side roads to the east, toward the lakeshore, are worth exploring. They take you through cedar woods and past small farms, with glimpses of the open lake and the occasional limestone cliff.

Summer weekends are crowded, particularly around the restaurant with the goats, so aim to arrive early. Autumn brings the colours, with the maples turning vivid red and gold by early October, and the crowds drift back to the cities. Spring is cool and wet, but the cherry blossoms are worth the cold. Pack a warm layer for the evening, because the air off the bay can be sharp even after a hot day.
t.door county coastal byway point 5@45.3,-:
Gills Rock is where Door County runs out of road, almost. It is a small fishing village at the northern tip of the peninsula, with a cluster of docks, a few weathered buildings and a view across the narrow strait to Washington Island. The strait itself, known as Death's Door, is notorious for its rough water and strong currents, and over the centuries it has swallowed many ships, from Native American canoes to nineteenth-century schooners. The French name Porte des Morts was the origin of the county's name.

The community here has a distinctly Norwegian heritage, and for generations its men made a living from commercial fishing, setting nets for whitefish and trout in the cold waters of the lake. A small maritime museum remembers the trade, with boats, nets and the stories of storm and rescue. You can still buy smoked fish at a few places nearby, and the smell of woodsmoke and fish is one of the characteristic scents of the village.

The riding here is the best of the peninsula in one respect: the farther north you go, the quieter the road becomes. Highway 42 narrows and runs through dense forest, with only a few houses and little traffic outside summer. The curves are gentle, but the canopy of trees gives the road a tunnel-like feel, and in autumn the colours form a bright roof. The surface is generally good, though frost heaves can appear after a hard winter.

Services are very limited. There is no reliable fuel in the village, so fill the tank in Sister Bay before you come, and carry food and water if you plan a long day. The ferry to Washington Island leaves from nearby Northport, a short distance east, and takes about thirty minutes, with vehicles carried on the deck. It makes a good excursion if you want to extend the ride.

Come on a still morning if you can. The water in the strait is flat as glass, the gulls are loud, and the fishing boats go out at first light. In the evening, the sun sinks behind the trees and the whole peninsula goes quiet. Weather can turn cold and foggy even in summer, so bring a warm layer, and in late autumn the northern tip is empty, with a wild feel that the busy summer villages lack.
t.near vads@70.1,30.1:
Ekkerøy is not quite an island: a low ridge of rock connected to the mainland by a narrow sandy isthmus, about fifteen kilometres east of Vadsø, with a small village on the sheltered side and a sheer bird cliff on the seaward side. In summer that cliff holds a colony of kittiwakes in the thousands, and the noise and smell of them reach you long before you see the nests, packed on every ledge above the waves.

The island is a nature reserve, and a footpath runs along the top of the cliffs, giving close views of the birds without disturbing them. Ekkerøy is also one of the places where the Varanger region's reputation among birdwatchers was built: the shore and the sea around it attract waders, ducks and seabirds, and in winter the rare Steller's eider gathers in the fjord. The beaches are covered with driftwood and shells, and the light here, especially in the long summer evenings, is clear and silvery.

The ridge has a long history of settlement. Archaeologists have found traces of Stone Age dwellings on the island, and there are remains of old fishing settlements along the shore. During the Second World War the Germans built fortifications here, part of the coastal defences of Finnmark, and you can still see bunkers and gun positions among the rocks. The village today is a quiet place of old houses and fishing sheds.

The road from Vadsø to Ekkerøy follows the shore of the Varangerfjord, flat and open, with gentle curves and wide views. The surface is good, and traffic is minimal. The wind can lean on you hard and cold, and the forecast can be wrong by lunchtime. This is a ride for the atmosphere rather than the corners: the landscape is wide and empty, the sea is grey or silver, and the sky is enormous.

Ekkerøy has no real services beyond a few houses. Vadsø, about fifteen kilometres back toward the west, has fuel, shops and cafes. Take binoculars if you have them, walk along the cliff path, and give the birds plenty of room. In late June and early July, when the chicks hatch, the colony is at its most lively.
t.vard@70.4,31.1:
Vardø is the easternmost town in Norway, further east than Istanbul, sitting on a small island off the tip of the Varanger peninsula and connected to the mainland by an undersea tunnel, the first of its kind in the country when it opened in 1982. The town is small and weathered, with a harbour full of fishing boats, colourful houses, abandoned buildings and an air of having seen better days, but it has a powerful history and a few sights that are worth the long ride.

Vardøhus, the octagonal star fortress built in the eighteenth century, is the northernmost fortress in the world and still garrisoned, with ramparts you can walk on and a rowan tree that the soldiers nurse through the harsh winters. Vardø also has a darker past. In the seventeenth century, dozens of people, most of them women, were accused of witchcraft and burned at the stake here, in one of the worst witch-hunts in Norwegian history. The Steilneset Memorial, a long timber and fabric structure designed by Peter Zumthor, with a glass pavilion containing an installation by Louise Bourgeois, commemorates them on the shore where the fires burned. It counts as one of the most moving monuments in Scandinavia.

For centuries, Vardø was a centre of the Pomor trade, when Russian merchants from the White Sea came to buy fish in exchange for grain and goods, and the town has a long relationship with Russia, visible in its history and architecture. Out in the sea, the bird island of Hornøya, reached by boat, hosts huge colonies of puffins, guillemots and kittiwakes in summer, and it counts among the best places in Europe to watch seabirds up close.

The road to Vardø follows the coast from Vadsø, part of the Varanger National Tourist Route, and it is long, open and atmospheric, with views over the sea and tundra. The surface is generally good, and traffic is light. The wind can be fierce, and showers come through with little notice.

Vardø has fuel, shops, a few cafes and accommodation. Beyond the town the road continues north along the coast to Hamningberg, an abandoned fishing village at the end of the road, open only in summer. Bring warm clothes and plenty of time.
